editorial.headline: Private General Junior Secondary Education: Open Nationally, Viable in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A private junior secondary education activity open to full foreign ownership nationally, with Bali’s moratorium not blocking it at large-scale risk.
editorial.body:
This activity covers privately run general junior secondary education for learners aged 13 to 15, together with related equivalency education. Its centre of gravity is broad learning in science and general skills: the familiar work of a private junior secondary school, but also private special-needs junior secondary education and private Paket B provision. The scope also accommodates formal educational cooperation between an accredited or recognised foreign educational institution and an Indonesian educational institution, provided it operates within the applicable formal-education framework.

The registrant is, in practical terms, the private education provider establishing or managing the junior secondary unit. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the record does not confine it to a single size of operator. That breadth matters because this is an education activity defined by the institution and the learning it provides, rather than by a narrow delivery format. A provider may be operating a conventional private school, a specialised junior secondary school, an equivalency programme, or a formal cross-border educational collaboration within the stated scope.

Nationally, the PMA position is clear: the activity is TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. In Bali, it is not blocked by the province-wide moratorium. The record places the OSS risk at Besar scale in the Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi range, rather than the Low or Medium-Low categories covered by that moratorium. Bali’s status is therefore OK_or_HIGHER_RISK: a foreign-owned registration is not shut out by the island-wide rule, while the record expressly signals the higher-risk profile at large scale.

That distinction is the useful one for founders. This is not an activity whose national openness disappears on arrival in Bali. It remains foreign-open nationally at the stated ceiling, and Bali does not block it under the moratorium described in the record. The operational question is instead whether the intended institution genuinely fits this private junior-secondary educational scope, including its age group, general-learning orientation, and—where relevant—the formal structure of cooperation with an overseas educational institution.
